Hint: Use the total who like at least one, then apply three-set inclusion-exclusion; for exactly two, subtract the triple overlap from each pairwise intersection.
Explanation: First n(A∪B∪C)=1400−110=1290. Inclusion-exclusion gives n(A∩B∩C)=20. Exactly two equals (350−20)+(290−20)+(370−20)=950. The distractors come from using a pairwise intersection without removing the triple overlap, or stopping at the union count. Wrong-option audit: Option B: using a pairwise intersection as the triple overlap.  Option C: failing to remove the triple overlap when counting exactly two.  Option D: stopping at the at-least-one count.

Question: In a mapping worksheet, A is the source set and R is a collection of ordered pairs. For A={1, 2, 3} and R={(1,2), (2,2), (3,1)}, is R a binary relation on A?
Option B: No, because R must equal A×A
Option D: No, because ordered pairs must have distinct components

Explanation: A binary relation on A is any subset of A×A. Every listed pair has both components in A, so R⊆A×A and R is binary. Wrong-option audit: Option B: requiring R=A×A instead of R⊆A×A.  Option C: requiring an unnecessary diagonal pair.  Option D: requiring every domain element to occur.
